waypoints.name: Harts Pass Trailhead (PCT North Trailhead)
waypoints.note: Reached via 20-mile gravel FS-5400 from Mazama; self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk before heading north on the PCT.
waypoints.directions: FS-5400 runs about 20 miles of narrow gravel from Mazama up to the pass, with steep drop-offs and no guardrail, and it stays snowed in well into early summer. At roughly 6,200 ft this is the highest drivable pass in Washington, so the trip opens as a rolling high traverse rather than a climb.

waypoints.name: Holman Pass
waypoints.note: Low point of the traverse where the PCT meets Holman Pass Trail; a spring and campsite lie a short way north before the climb toward Rock Pass.
waypoints.directions: Head north on the PCT over Windy Pass and the Tamarack/Foggy/Jim Pass group, traversing beneath Jim Peak's Devils Backbone. It rolls constantly rather than climbing, and finishes by giving back about 1,100 ft into the pass — roughly 14 miles with a couple of thousand feet of gain and slightly more loss.

waypoints.name: Rock Pass
waypoints.note: Open scree pass roughly 3.2 mi past Holman Pass; the trail crosses a north-facing scree slope here near the Rock Creek Trail 473 junction down to the Pasayten River.
waypoints.directions: Climb steadily back out of the low point, gaining about 1,400 ft in a little over three miles. The trail crosses a north-facing scree slope just before the pass which holds snow later than the trail either side of it.

waypoints.name: Woody Pass
waypoints.note: Treeless, exposed saddle despite the name, about 2.7 mi beyond Rock Pass; short climb north leads toward Devils Stairway.
waypoints.directions: Under three miles of high, open traversing with modest gain. Despite the name there is no tree cover on this section, so it is fully exposed to wind and to afternoon storms — there is nowhere to sit one out between here and Castle Pass.

waypoints.name: Castle Pass
waypoints.note: PCT/Boundary Trail junction roughly 27 mi from Harts Pass; leave the PCT here and follow the Boundary Trail east/north toward Frosty Pass instead of continuing to Monument 78.
waypoints.directions: The longest stretch of the traverse: north past the Devils Stairway switchbacks and Hopkins Lake to Hopkins Pass, then down roughly 1,200 ft to Castle Pass. Water and camping at the pass itself are poor and the nearest reliable water is about a mile away down in Route Creek Basin, which is worth knowing before you arrive late in the day.

waypoints.name: Frosty Pass
waypoints.note: Gateway pass on the Boundary Trail east of Castle Pass; the maintained tread ends here and the trail-free scramble toward Blizzard Peak and Mt. Winthrop begins.
waypoints.directions: Turn off the PCT onto the Boundary Trail and climb east, about four miles with a couple of substantial pulls, traversing below Mount Winthrop's west slopes. Tread beyond Castle Pass is unmaintained and thins out, so route-finding across the open slopes is part of this leg rather than an exception on it.

waypoints.name: Upper Frosty Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Roomy trailside camp with water nearby just below Frosty Pass; a faint boot path breaks off to the right (westbound) to reach the best tent sites.
waypoints.directions: Drop several hundred feet off the pass into the basin's grassy flats. This is the last dependable water until you are back out, so fill here — and leave the overnight gear, since the peak is climbed as an out-and-back from camp with a light pack.

waypoints.name: Blizzard Peak Summit
waypoints.note: Broad Class 1-2 talus/rock summit block reached by ascending open terrain from Frosty Pass/Upper Frosty Basin; views north into Manning Provincial Park, BC and across to Mt. Winthrop.
waypoints.directions: Climb back to Frosty Pass and head off-trail south, gaining Blizzard's broad north ridge and following it up open talus, heather benches and blocky rock. It is sustained Class 1-2 with no route-finding crux in good visibility, but there is nothing to follow in fog, and the ridge and upper basin hold snow into early summer — worth carrying an axe for a June or early-July attempt. Mount Winthrop is the common same-day add-on, reached in the opposite direction from the pass.

waypoints.name: Andrews Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk; trail #504 starts in a 2003-burn zone with little shade for the first several miles.
waypoints.directions: Drive West Chewuch Road / FR-51 north out of Winthrop roughly 22-23 miles to the road end at about 3,050 ft. Everything above is gained on foot — this is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state, and the Chewuch River trailhead to the east is a longer alternative to the same camp.

waypoints.name: Andrews Creek (burn-zone crossings)
waypoints.note: Trail parallels and repeatedly crosses Andrews Creek through the burn — last easy, frequent water before the climb toward the pass.
waypoints.directions: Trail #504 climbs steadily up the Andrews Creek drainage through the 2003 burn scar: little shade, brushy regrowth that soaks you through after rain, and blowdown between trail-crew visits. The creek runs beside the tread for these miles, so there is no reason to carry much water on this stretch.

waypoints.name: Peepsight Trail junction
waypoints.note: Stay on Andrews Creek Trail (left/straight) for Andrews Pass; the right fork climbs to Peepsight Lake.
waypoints.directions: Stay on #504 as it continues up-valley. The Peepsight Trail branches off toward Peepsight Creek and eventually rejoins the Andrews Creek line much higher by a far longer loop — not the way to Cathedral. Burn and brushy tread continue past the fork.

waypoints.name: Andrews Pass
waypoints.note: Burn zone ends and open meadow country begins here; dispersed camps sit on the bluff just east of the pass, trail then contours toward Spanish Creek and the Boundary Trail.
waypoints.directions: Above the Peepsight fork the trail keeps grinding up the drainage in burned timber until it tops out at the pass, where open parkland and meadow replace the snags and the view opens north toward Amphitheater Mountain. Snow patches can hold on this stretch into early July.

waypoints.name: Upper Cathedral Lake camp
waypoints.note: Established basecamp used by SE Buttress climbers, in parkland meadows just west of Cathedral Pass; last reliable water before the route.
waypoints.directions: From the pass follow the Boundary Trail (#533) through rolling meadow toward Spanish Creek, then take the Cathedral Lakes side trail, which bears off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin, for the last few miles into the lake basin. Budget a full, long day from the car to here; most parties arrive mid-afternoon.

waypoints.name: Cathedral Pass
waypoints.note: 40-60 min walk from camp; the Pacific Northwest Trail crosses here between Cathedral Peak and Amphitheater Mountain — leave the trail toward the Cathedral-Monk gully.
waypoints.directions: A 40-60 minute walk from camp, climbing east out of the lake basin on the trail that crosses the pass between Cathedral Peak and Amphitheater Mountain. Leave it at the first switchback above the pass and start up toward the gully.

waypoints.name: Cathedral–Monk gully approach
waypoints.note: Loose, wide gully separating Cathedral Peak from The Monk; route starts about 150 ft up it — watch for rockfall from other parties above.
waypoints.directions: Cross meadow and talus toward the obvious deep cleft between Cathedral Peak and the pinnacle called The Monk. There is no climbers' path, so pick the line by eye — 30 to 60 minutes from camp in total. Scramble up into the gully; the first pitch is on the left (north) wall a short way in, launched from a tall pedestal that makes a solid belay stance.

waypoints.name: Cathedral Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit atop the route's two-pitch headwall; descend trending west then southwest, 4th-class with an exposed gap crossing, back down into the meadows above Upper Cathedral Lake.
waypoints.directions: Ten pitches up the buttress: corners, a chockstone and chimney ground low down, easier discontinuous terrain through the middle, then the sustained headwall — linking pitches 8 and 9 into one 55-60 m lead avoids the route's only semi-hanging belay. Two short hand-crack steps and third-class scrambling finish at the true summit.

waypoints.name: Snow Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: 4.2 mi south on Icicle Creek Rd (FR-76) from junction with US-2, Leavenworth.
waypoints.directions: From Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road (Forest Road 7600) about 4.2 to 4.3 miles to the Snow Lakes Trailhead, at roughly 1,350 feet. Park in the lot on the south side of the road at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Nada Lake
waypoints.directions: Snow Lakes Trail #1553 crosses Icicle Creek and climbs steadily through forest up the Snow Creek drainage on long, relentless switchbacks to Nada Lake, with a loud creek just above it that is a reliable water source.

waypoints.name: Snow Lakes basin
waypoints.directions: Continue past Nada Lake to Lower and Upper Snow Lakes. The crossing on the logjam between the two lakes is the known hazard here, worst at high water or on a pre-dawn start.

waypoints.name: Leave the trail between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes
waypoints.directions: Above the Snow Lakes the tread becomes a rougher climbers' path that switchbacks steeply into the core Enchantments basin past Lake Viviane to Leprechaun Lake, near 7,000 ft. Leave the trail at the flat, open ground by Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes; there is no reliable water beyond the lakes.

waypoints.name: McClellan Peak summit
waypoints.directions: Climb steep talus, scree or snow, often firm and icy late in the season, to the crest of McClellan Ridge, keeping west of the rock tower called the Prong; drifting farther west into the Chessman towers dead-ends. From the crest, drop a short way and wrap onto the south side of the peak, then scramble Class 3 rock to the summit.

waypoints.name: Alpental Parking Lot
waypoints.note: Park at Alpental ski area (I-90 Exit 52); take the Source Lake trail, then head into the basin below The Tooth's east face.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 Exit 52 and follow Alpental Road about a mile and a half north to its end at the Alpental / Snow Lake trailhead, parking in the Alpental ski area lot at roughly 3,100 ft. The Source Lake trail leaves from the lot, and in winter you are hiking or skinning from the car. Read the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast before you drive up — the basin you approach through is avalanche terrain and that read is a pre-trip requirement, not an option.

waypoints.name: The Tooth
waypoints.note: Steeper winter variation on the east face (AI3-4/M4-5) reaching the same summit as the standard South Face route.
